newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: After APEC, what next for triumphant Ramos?.
newsitem.headline: After APEC, what next for triumphant Ramos?.

text.p: Even his staunchest critics already concede the APEC summit is a triumph for Philippine President Fidel Ramos, but warn he should not use it as a springboard to defy the constitution and extend his term of office.
"The only question left is whether this is the cue for him to exit in a blaze of glory or the prelude for the Ramos II presidency," Manila Standard columnist Nelson Navarro wrote.
Ramos played host on Monday to U.S. President Bill Clinton, fresh from his election victory, and other leaders attending the fourth annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit.

Ramos supporters see the event as a grand coming out party marking what economists view as a remarkable economic turnaround for the Philippines, using precisely the free market policies APEC is meant to espouse.
Critics, in Navarro's words, see it as "the quintessential vanity production".

When Ramos took office in 1992, the country was in the grip of a power crisis brought on by years of neglect and had flat growth after decades of authoritarian rule followed by political upheaval and a series of natural disasters.

Government planners expect growth this year to be more than 7.0 percent and billions of dollars worth of investments are pouring in, including about $2 billion in business generated by a private sector conference linked to APEC.
Foreign delegates to APEC have seen for themselves the evidence of new prosperity -- dozens of construction sites dotting this decayed, ramshackle capital.
Ramos, a workaholic West Point graduate, veteran of both the Korean and Vietnam wars and a former armed forces chief, is unlikely to spend much time basking in any post-APEC glory.
"I have many more duties apart from APEC," he gruffly told an inquisitor at one of his frequent news conferences.
Ramos, 68, has repeatedly denied he is looking for a way to get round the single six-year term the constitution provides so he can remain in office.
Members of his Lakas party, however, have been garnering signatures to a petition which would set in motion procedures to amend the constitution, allowing a reelection bid.
Another possibility, government insiders say, would be to pass a law postponing the next elections, due in 1998, to the year 2000.
One of the reasons many suspect Ramos would go along with this if it succeeded is the shortage of credible presidential candidates for 1998 and the need to ensure continuity of the current reforms.
A former Ramos press secretary, Jess Sison, wrote in a Malaya newspaper column that a recent survey of voters showed Ramos a clear favourite should he able to run again.
The prospect sends chills down the spines of many Filipinos, reminding them of the tactics used by the late President Ferdinand Marcos to cling onto power.
Marcos ended up using martial law to stay in office, jailing and torturing opponents.
Ramos would risk squandering the fruits of his considerable labours if he tried to remain in office, one columnist wrote.
"(Ramos) should not waste all of that by running again in 1998, against the very spirit of the constitution he had fought to preserve", wrote Bingo Dejaresco in the Philippine Star.
